historical_record.description: Theater operator Samuel H. Levin bought the five vacant lots that became the El Rey site from Fernando Nelson & Sons, developer of Mt. Davidson Manor, and held them as land for future development.
The El Rey Theater, designed by Miller and Pflueger.

The El Rey Theater opened with 1,800 seats and a screening of Maurice Chevalier in The Smiling Lieutenant; it cost $500,000 to build and fit out, double the first estimate, and was the first major movie theater west of Twin Peaks.
The theater's tower of nearly 150 feet was topped by a revolving airplane beacon and directional light pointing aircraft to Mills Field, now San Francisco International Airport.
El Rey Supermarket opened in the theater's west retail wing, where it traded until 1977; the building's eight original storefronts also held El Rey Pharmacy, a dress shop and El Rey Beauty Shop.
Samuel Levin's San Francisco Theatres, Inc. sold the El Rey Theater to El Rey Enterprises, a real estate holding company that hired managers to run it.
Fire damaged the rear of the coffee shop in the theater building's storefront at 1962 Ocean Avenue; a repair permit was sought that month.
The El Rey was fitted with an improved sound system and CinemaScope projection.
The original flat storefront canopy was replaced with the folded-plate canopy still in place, and the upper windows of the retail wings behind their decorative grilles were removed.
The first store of The Gap opened in the El Rey building's east storefront, selling Levi's jeans, records and tapes; the company closed it in 1974.

COYOTE, the sex workers' rights organisation founded by Margo St. James, held its second International Hookers' Film Festival at the El Rey, four days of more than 40 films; the theater closed after it.
El Rey Enterprises sold the closed theater to Voice of Pentecost, an evangelical church that converted it into its sanctuary, school and offices.
The former El Rey Supermarket space in the west retail wing was converted into a Sunday school, removing the wing's original storefronts.
The storefronts along Ocean Avenue were refaced with imitation fieldstone bulkheads and new steel windows.
Robert Durden photographed the property, showing Voice of the Pentecost Church and El Rey Theater.
After the church defaulted on its mortgage, the former theater was sold at public auction for $1,060,000.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 274, El Rey Theater.

notable_residents.detail: Samuel H. Levin, the neighborhood theater developer who built the Haight, Coliseum, Balboa and Harding theaters, bought this site and built the El Rey through his company San Francisco Theatres, Inc., which owned it until 1938.
